## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 55 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** Chapter 6 (@sec-dependencies), for the
renv lockfile and the union model this chapter extends to
a team, and Chapter 7 (@sec-containers), for the
digest-pinned Docker image this chapter archives and whose
guarantee it relocates from the image to the Dockerfile.
Chapter 3 (@sec-levels), for the L0-L3 ladder every honest
claim in this chapter is stated against. Chapter 4
(@sec-version-control), for the commit rule this chapter's
restricted-data section makes stricter. No new statistical
knowledge is assumed; reading a Dockerfile and a short
shell session is.

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to
answer:**

- Can you explain the two-layer team model and decide
  which layer a given package decision belongs to under
  the renv union model?
- Can you state why the committed Dockerfile, and not the
  pushed image, is the reproducibility guarantee, and
  choose a registry and a forge with vendor independence
  in view?
- Can you deposit a research compendium for the long
  term, minting a persistent identifier and archiving the
  environment as a single file, and relate the steps to
  the FAIR principles?
- Can you recover a decayed environment from the date an
  analysis was run, and state the sustainability limits
  of a young framework honestly rather than papering over
  them?
- Can you adapt the sharing-and-archiving workflow to a
  package, a blog, and a manuscript, naming what varies
  and what does not?

**Outline.**

- Orientation: a laboratory whose environment nobody can
  reconstruct two years later.
- The analyst's contribution: three judgments no tool
  automates.
- Where this sits on the stack: what archiving captures
  and what it only validates.
- Sharing with a team: the two-layer model.
- Sharing with the world: archiving, and what changes
  when the data are restricted.
- Stewardship over time: recovering a decayed
  environment.
- Across the archetypes: package, blog, manuscript.
- Worked example: one laboratory's quarter of
  collaboration and one deposit.
- The cohort, continued: checking this book's own
  compendium against a deposit checklist, today.
- Collaborating with an LLM.
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

This chapter pins no layer of the determinant stack for
the first time; both of its halves, sharing with a team
and archiving with the world, are stated as adding no new
rung. Yet it is not neutral with respect to the stack
either, and the two things it does are different in kind.

@fig-stack-archiving marks both. Archiving is the first
point in the book where the *input data* layer moves from
merely locatable in a team's repository, which a forge
outage or a departed contributor can erase, to durably
findable under a persistent identifier that continues to
resolve after the project ends. No earlier chapter made
that move, so it is marked as captured here even though it
pins no new version and fixes no new byte. Stewardship, by
contrast, pins nothing new about the packages or the
operating system; the union lockfile and the digest-pinned
image already did that capturing in @sec-dependencies and
@sec-containers. What stewardship does is confirm, using
`rang` or an archived image, that those pins can still be
resolved after they have aged, which is validation of a
layer already captured elsewhere rather than a fresh
capture of its own.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stack-archiving
#| fig-cap: 'The determinant stack of @sec-levels, with input data marked as captured here and the package-version and operating-system layers marked as validated. This chapter pins no new byte: the packages are captured in @sec-dependencies and the operating system in @sec-containers. What it adds to the data layer is durability, lifting it from merely locatable on a forge to findable under a persistent identifier, which is why input data is captured rather than validated here; what it adds to the package and system layers is the stewardship check, using an archived image or a date-based reconstruction, that those earlier pins still resolve, which is why they are validated rather than captured again.'
#| fig-alt: !expr determinant_stack_alt(captures = c('Input data'), validates = c('Package versions', 'Operating system, system libraries'))
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
plot_determinant_stack(
  captures = c('Input data'),
  validates = c('Package versions',
                'Operating system, system libraries'),
  title = 'Where archiving and stewardship sit on the stack'
)
```

## Orientation

We arrive at the last question a reproducible analysis
must answer, and it is not a technical question but a
social and temporal one. Every earlier chapter was
concerned with a single machine and a single analyst:
how to pin the packages (@sec-dependencies),
fix the environment (@sec-containers), render the
report (@sec-literate), and validate the whole with
tests and continuous integration (@sec-verification).
The present chapter concerns what happens when the
analysis must leave that machine. It must first reach
a collaborator down the hall, and eventually reach a
stranger, a reviewer, or the analyst's own future self,
years after the original laptop has been recycled.

Consider a concrete case. A five-person laboratory
runs a multi-site observational cohort. The
principal investigator fixes the computational
environment at the project's start; over the following
year, one contributor adds survival-analysis packages,
a second adds table-formatting packages for the
manuscript, and a third adds spatial packages for a
geographic sub-study. Each installs freely, on their
own machine, without asking the others' permission.
Two years after the paper appears, a journal requests
the analysis for a reproducibility audit, and the
original environment must be reconstructed from
whatever survives in the repository. Nothing in the
single-analyst workflow of the earlier chapters tells
us how the laboratory should have coordinated during
that year, nor how the compendium should have been
deposited so that the audit could succeed.

These are two distinct problems, and we shall keep
them apart. The first is collaboration: sharing a
compendium with a team while it is under active
development, so that contributors do not drift into
mutually incompatible environments. The second is
archiving and stewardship: depositing the finished
compendium so that it remains findable and executable
long after the project ends, and recovering it when
the pins have decayed. Both sit at the top of the
reproducibility ladder rather than adding a new rung.
Sharing a compendium changes nothing about its
level: an L2 compendium shared with a team is still an
L2 compendium, and a verified L3 compendium deposited
in an archive is still L3. What sharing and archiving
add is the assurance that the level already reached
survives contact with other people and with the
passage of time. That assurance is the subject of this
chapter, and, being the last chapter, it is also where
we draw the threads of the whole book together.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two problems, not one

The laboratory's L2 compendium is shared with a new
contributor, who extends the package layer, and is later
deposited in Zenodo. Does either event change the level
the compendium has reached? What does each event add if
not a level?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Neither event changes the level. Sharing the compendium
with a new contributor, and depositing it with a DOI, are
both social and temporal acts, not capture acts: the
compendium was L2 before either happened and remains L2
afterward. What sharing adds is that the fixed environment
survives contact with a second person without drifting;
what archiving adds is that the fixed environment survives
the passage of time and the disappearance of the original
machine. Both are about the level already reached
surviving, not about reaching a new one.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Three judgments in this chapter are the analyst's own,
and no tool makes them.

1. **Where to draw the governance boundary, between
   what the team fixes and what each member may vary.**
   The framework offers the two-layer model as a
   default, but only a person who understands the
   project can decide which layer a given decision
   belongs to. Fixing too much makes the team rigid and
   slows every contributor; fixing too little lets the
   environment fracture. The base image, the R version,
   and the system libraries are almost always the
   lead's to fix; the analysis packages are almost
   always the members' to add. The awkward cases in
   between, a version of a system library that one
   sub-study needs and the others do not, are decided
   by the analyst, not the tool.

2. **When to deposit, at what depth, and at what level
   to claim.** An archival deposit is a public and
   permanent act, and the honest disclosure of the
   level reached is part of the deposit, not an
   afterthought. Depositing a compendium and labeling
   it 'reproducible' without stating whether it has
   been verified, or whether the environment was pinned
   by digest or merely by tag, misrepresents the work.
   The analyst decides when the compendium is ready,
   which artifacts accompany it, which data the consent
   and the data-use agreement allow to accompany it,
   and, above all, what the accompanying claim honestly
   says.

3. **Where the work lives, and how dependent that
   choice makes it.** A registry and a forge are
   conveniences, but each is also a dependency on a
   commercial vendor whose terms may change. The
   analyst weighs the convenience of a popular platform
   against the vendor independence of an institutional
   or self-hosted alternative, and does so knowing that
   a compendium tied to a service that disappears is a
   compendium at risk.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Registry.** A server that stores and distributes
  container images, from which collaborators pull a
  pre-built environment. GitHub Container Registry
  (GHCR) and Docker Hub are the two in common use.
- **Forge.** A platform that hosts a version-controlled
  repository and runs its continuous integration.
  GitHub and GitLab are the two principal forges;
  GitLab is frequently self-hosted by universities.
- **Two-layer team model.** A division of a project
  into a slow-moving environment layer, fixed once by a
  team lead, and a fast-moving package layer, extended
  by every contributor.
- **Union model.** The rule that the project lockfile
  records the union of every package any contributor
  has installed, so that a rebuilt image carries what
  the whole team needs, not only what one member used.
- **Persistent identifier (DOI).** A durable, resolvable
  name for a deposited artifact, such as a Digital
  Object Identifier, that continues to resolve even if
  the artifact moves.
- **FAIR.** A set of principles holding that a research
  object should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable,
  and Reusable, formulated for data and later adapted
  for research software.
- **OCI tarball or SIF file.** A container image exported
  as a single file, checksummable and depositable as an
  archival artifact. An OCI image is exported as a tar
  archive, whereas SIF is the self-contained single-file
  format used by the Apptainer runtime.
- **Zenodo.** A general-purpose research repository,
  operated at CERN, that mints a DOI for any deposited
  file set.
- **Controlled access.** A repository arrangement in
  which data are released only to approved users under
  an agreement, rather than to anyone who downloads.
- **Data-availability statement.** The statement in an
  article or README of what was deposited, where, and
  how any data not deposited may be obtained.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: whose judgment, again

A compendium is ready to deposit, by every mechanical
check: the tests pass, the lockfile is current, the image
builds. Name one judgment from this section that a
checklist still cannot make, and say why it cannot.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A checklist cannot decide what level to claim in the
accompanying statement. It can confirm that a lockfile and
a Dockerfile exist, which is mechanical, but it cannot
decide whether the analyst has actually re-run the
pipeline from a clean rebuild and compared the outputs, nor
can it know what the consent and data-use agreement permit
to accompany the deposit. Those are judgments about this
specific project's history and its governing documents,
and no tool has access to either.
:::
:::

## Sharing with a team: the two-layer model

We begin with the collaboration problem, and with the
observation that motivates the whole design: the two
things a team shares change at very different rates.
The computational environment, the operating system,
the R version, and the system libraries, is chosen at
most a handful of times over the life of a project. The
set of R packages, by contrast, changes almost weekly
as the analysis grows. A model that forces both to be
renegotiated on the same schedule will either freeze
the packages to the cadence of the environment, which
is too slow, or churn the environment to the cadence of
the packages, which is too disruptive. The resolution,
adopted by the framework this book uses and set out by
its authors, is to separate the two into layers with
different change rates and different governance.

**Layer 1 is the environment, and it is lead-governed.**
A designated team lead selects a base image at the
project's start, resolves it to an immutable content
digest, and fixes it for every collaborator. This is
the slow-moving half. It corresponds to pillar one, the
computational environment, and it is where the L1-to-L2
transition of the ladder is secured. The lead builds
this environment once, and the whole team reuses it. the vignette that describes the pattern calls this
'build once, use everywhere', and reports that reusing
a pre-built team image reduces the setup of a new
project from the fifteen or twenty minutes of a full
build to a matter of seconds. The saving is real, but
it is not the point that matters most for
reproducibility. The point that matters is that every
collaborator works from the same fixed floor.

**Layer 2 is the package set, and it is
contributor-governed under the union model.** Each
member installs the packages their part of the work
requires, freely and without coordination, and the
project lockfile at any moment records the *union* of
everything anyone has installed. When the shared image
is rebuilt from that lockfile, periodically rather than
on every change, it carries the full set every
contributor needs, not merely the subset one member
happened to use. A collaborator who pulls the latest
main branch and rebuilds therefore inherits the survival
packages, the table packages, and the spatial packages
all at once, whether or not their own work touches any
of them. This is the fast-moving half, corresponding to
pillar two, and it is governed by every member rather
than by the lead.

The union model buys the elimination of a common and
maddening failure, the analysis that runs for its author
and nowhere else, at the price of a little environmental
bloat. A package installed once for an exploratory
notebook remains in the lockfile for everyone until it
is deliberately removed. In our view this is a sound
trade. On the one hand, the bloat is bounded and
visible, a few extra megabytes in an image that is
already a gigabyte or more, and it can be pruned when it
matters. On the other, the failure it prevents,
a contributor blocked because a colleague forgot to
record a dependency, is the precise 'works on my
machine' pathology that the whole enterprise exists to
abolish. We would rather carry an unused package than
lose a day to a missing one.

### The Dockerfile, not the image, is the guarantee

Here we must state a principle that is easy to get
backwards. The pushed team image is a convenience, a
cache that saves build time; it is *not* the
reproducibility guarantee. The guarantee is the
Dockerfile, together with the lockfile it restores from,
both committed to version control. The reason is that a
pushed image is opaque and impermanent: it is a binary
blob on a registry that may be deleted, may be pruned
under a retention policy, may be pushed for one
processor architecture and silently emulated on another,
and cannot be inspected line by line to see how it was
made. The Dockerfile is transparent and durable: it is a
text recipe, readable and diffable, that reconstructs
the image from named and pinned inputs. If the registry
vanishes tomorrow, a compendium whose guarantee is the
Dockerfile can be rebuilt; a compendium whose guarantee
was the pushed image cannot.

The framework's vignette makes the same point in a note
that is worth restating in our terms: pushing the image
to a registry is optional, and if the image is not
available, building from the Dockerfile reproduces the
environment. We should qualify that claim, in keeping
with this chapter's own discipline: a rebuild reproduces
the same content, the same base image, R version, and
package versions, only when the base image is pinned by
content digest and the package snapshot is dated, as
@sec-containers urged; a recipe pinned by a mutable tag,
or drawing on a rolling snapshot, reconstructs at best a
functionally equivalent environment whose content may
have drifted. Even a correctly digest-pinned,
dated-snapshot rebuild is not guaranteed byte-for-byte
identical at the image level, because per-layer
timestamps ordinarily differ between builds; matching
content is the guarantee a pinned recipe gives, and
bit-identical bytes require separate reproducible-build
tooling (@sec-containers). The image is the fast path;
the recipe is the guarantee of content, not of bytes.
A team that treats the pushed image as authoritative,
and lets the Dockerfile drift
out of step with it, has quietly converted its
compendium from something reconstructable into something
that merely happens to exist, which is exactly the
regression to L0 that honest disclosure is meant to
catch.

### Registries and the forge

Two distribution choices attend team sharing, and both
are best understood as concerns about vendor
independence rather than about reproducibility level.
Neither changes the level a compendium has reached.

The **registry** is where the team image is published:
GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, or an
institutional registry such as one hosted inside GitLab.
Docker Hub is the most familiar, but its free tier rate-
limits image pulls and permits only a single private
repository, constraints that a small laboratory reaches
quickly. GHCR integrates with the GitHub forge and has
more generous terms for public research. An institution
with confidentiality requirements may mandate a private
or self-hosted registry. The choice is a trade between
convenience and control, and, we would stress, it is
reversible: because the guarantee is the Dockerfile, a
team can re-push its image to a different registry at any
time without altering the compendium.

The **forge** is where the repository and its continuous
integration live: GitHub, or, very often in the health
sciences, an institutional GitLab. This choice matters
more than it first appears, because research compendia
are disproportionately authored on self-hosted GitLab.
Many universities and laboratories, particularly those
subject to on-premises data-governance rules, run their
own GitLab and cannot push to a public forge. A
framework whose premise is reproducibility for that
audience must not lock its users into one forge. The
practical difficulty is concentrated entirely in
continuous integration: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI use
structurally different configuration dialects, so
supporting both without maintaining two parallel and
divergent sets of workflow files requires that the CI
logic be single-sourced, typically in the Makefile, with
each forge's configuration reduced to a thin shim that
calls it. The lesson for the analyst is to treat the
forge as a replaceable host, not as the home of the
work, and to keep the reproducibility logic in artifacts
that travel between forges unchanged.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what survives a registry outage

A colleague argues that the team should push its image
to Docker Hub after every package installation, 'so the
image is always the source of truth'. What is wrong with
treating the pushed image as the source of truth, and
what should be the source of truth instead?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The pushed image is an opaque, impermanent binary that
may be deleted, rate-limited, pruned, or built for the
wrong architecture, and it cannot be inspected to see
how it was made. If Docker Hub removes it, an analysis
that depended on it is lost. The source of truth should
be the committed Dockerfile together with the lockfile
it restores from: a transparent, diffable, durable
recipe that reconstructs an identical image from pinned
inputs. The image is a convenience cache; the recipe is
the guarantee. Pushing after every install also wastes
effort, since the image need only be rebuilt
periodically from the union lockfile.
:::
:::

## Sharing with the world: archiving

Sharing with a team keeps a live project consistent.
Archiving asks a different question: how does a finished
compendium survive after the project ends, the
collaborators disperse, and the laboratory's servers are
decommissioned? A repository on a forge is not an
archive. Forges delete inactive accounts, rename
themselves, change ownership, and go out of business; a
URL that resolves today may not resolve in a decade. An
archive, by contrast, undertakes to preserve a deposit
and to keep a name for it resolving indefinitely.

The instrument is a deposit in a research repository
that mints a **persistent identifier**. Depositing the
compendium in Zenodo, the general-purpose repository
operated at CERN, produces a Digital Object Identifier
that continues to resolve even as the underlying storage
moves, and that can be cited in the article the
compendium supports. The DOI is what lifts a compendium
from merely locatable on a forge, which is fragile, to
durably findable, which is the archival requirement.

A deposit should carry the environment, not only the
source. Here the container runtimes of @sec-backends
supply exactly the archival artifact needed. Apptainer,
the high-performance-computing runtime, builds from a
digest-pinned Docker image a single Singularity Image
Format file, and that SIF, or equivalently an OCI image
exported as a tarball, is checksummable and depositable
as one object. A compendium archived as its source tree
plus a pinned Dockerfile plus the built environment as a
single file is reproducible by two independent routes: a
reader may rebuild from the recipe, or, if the recipe's
inputs have decayed, may run the archived environment
directly. Depositing both is belt and braces, and for a
result that matters it is worth the disk. What a deposit
may carry of the *data* is a separate question, governed
by the terms under which the data were obtained rather
than by the analyst's wish to be reproducible; for
patient-level data the usual answer is that the data stay
out of an open deposit, and @sec-restricted-deposit
treats what is deposited in their place.

These practices realize a set of principles that the
community has crystallized under the acronym FAIR.
Wilkinson and colleagues proposed that a research object
should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and
Reusable, and framed the principles for research data
[@wilkinson2016]. Barker and colleagues subsequently
adapted them for research software, whose reuse involves
execution and not only reading [@barker2022]. A DOI
serves findability; a repository with a stated access
procedure serves accessibility, which for restricted
data means a controlled route rather than an open
download; a documented, standard container format
serves interoperability; and a pinned, rebuildable
environment serves part of reusability. Reusability
also requires a clear usage license (R1.1 in the
original principles), which a pinned environment does
not by itself supply. The archetype-agnostic compendium
of @sec-compendium is, in this light, most of the way to
a FAIR object by construction, provided it is deposited
rather than merely committed and carries an explicit
license; licensing practice is treated separately.

### Licensing, CITATION.cff, and Software Heritage

A pinned environment and a minted DOI satisfy three of
FAIR's four letters without touching the fourth's hardest
requirement. Reusability, principle R1.1 in the original
statement, asks for 'a clear and accessible data usage
license' [@wilkinson2016], and nothing about findability,
accessibility, or interoperability supplies one: a
compendium can be perfectly findable and still carry no
statement of what a reader is permitted to do with it,
which in the absence of a license defaults, under
copyright, to nothing. 'The cohort, continued' below
returns to what license this book's own compendium
carries.

Two further instruments round out what a deposit should
carry, beyond the license file itself.

**CITATION.cff.** A `CITATION.cff` file is a plain-text,
machine-readable citation record placed at a repository's
root, using a small set of `key: value` fields
(`cff-version`, `authors`, `title`, `version`, and
`date-released` among them) [@githubcitationfiles2024].
GitHub parses the file, when it sits on the default branch,
into a 'Cite this repository' link on the repository page
that generates an APA or BibTeX citation on request
[@githubcitationfiles2024]. Zenodo reads the same file on
deposit and uses it to pre-fill the deposit's own citation
metadata, so a `CITATION.cff` written once serves both the
forge and the archive. Without it, a reader who wants to
cite the compendium constructs a citation by hand from
whatever metadata happens to be visible on the page, which
is the same fragility that motivated the DOI in the first
place.

**Software Heritage.** Zenodo is a deposit repository: an
institution, CERN, operates it, and while its continuation
is a reasonable expectation, it is an expectation and not a
guarantee, since a deposit repository could in principle be
discontinued by the institution that runs it. Software
Heritage undertakes something narrower and more absolute
for source code specifically: its stated mission is a
permanent, universal archive of publicly available source
code, with no depositor-facing mechanism to remove
something once archived. The project's own scale and its
SWHID identifier scheme were formalized as an ISO/IEC
standard in 2025 [@swhiso2025]. Every archived
object, whether a file, a directory, a commit, or a full
repository snapshot, receives a SoftWare Hash IDentifier of
the form `swh:1:<type>:<hash>`, where `<type>` names the
kind of object (`cnt` for a file's content, `dir` for a
directory, among others) and `<hash>` is a 40-character
value computed from the object's own bytes
[@swhmodeldocs2024]. Because the identifier is computed
from the content rather than assigned by a registry, two
copies of the same file anywhere in the archive resolve to
the same SWHID, which is a different kind of guarantee from
a DOI: a DOI names a deposit, and a SWHID names the bytes.

This book's own repository illustrates the gap between
having these instruments and using them well. A
`CITATION.cff` is present at the repository root, generated
by zzcollab when the project was created, but it still
carries an empty `orcid` field and the placeholder
affiliation `Your Institution`, unfilled at the time of
this writing. The file's presence is enough for GitHub to
render the 'Cite this repository' link and for Zenodo to
read it on deposit; its content is not yet enough to tell a
reader whom, exactly, to credit. Filling it in is a
five-minute task left to the lead, not a content addition
this chapter needs to make.

Two broader efforts are worth the analyst's attention.
The Whole Tale platform, described by Brinckman and
colleagues, bundles code, data, and computational
environment into a single executable research object
that a reader can run in the browser without local
installation [@brinckman2019], an ambition the
compendium-plus-archived-image pattern approaches by
other means. And the Turing Way, a community-authored
handbook, collects the collaborative and stewardship
practices of reproducible research into one continually
updated reference [@turingway2022]. A reader who wants
the social side of collaboration, from code review to
project governance to credit, in more depth than a
single chapter allows, should begin there.

### When the data are restricted {#sec-restricted-deposit}

Everything said so far about depositing assumes that every
file in the compendium may be published. In health
research that assumption is usually false. A compendium
built on patient records contains, or was built from, data
whose release is governed by law, by the consent the
participants gave, and by the data-use agreement under
which the analyst received the extract. A deposit in an
open repository is a publication to anyone, indefinitely,
and a file placed there cannot be recalled.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

The rule is the commit rule of @sec-version-control, made
stricter: patient-level data do not go into an open
deposit unless they have been formally de-identified, the
consent and the agreement both permit public release, and
the responsible data steward or IRB has confirmed it in
writing. In their place, a deposit may carry the code, the
tests, the lockfile, the Dockerfile, and the archived
image, always; de-identified data, only where the data's
steward has made that determination; a synthetic stand-in,
labeled as such; or, for data that may be shared under
agreement but not opened to the world, a citation to a
controlled-access repository such as dbGaP. None of these
substitutes removes the obligation to read the consent
form and the data-use agreement first, and the deposit's
data-availability statement must say, exactly, which of
these routes was taken.
:::

What remains is to work through each of the five routes
named above in enough detail to act on. There are five
parts to the answer.

**The code and the environment, always.** The analysis
code, the tests, the lockfile, the Dockerfile, and the
archived image carry no participant data, and depositing
them openly lets anyone inspect the analysis and lets
anyone who obtains the data by the legitimate route re-run
it. Two checks come first. The archived image must not
contain the data: a `COPY . .` executed while the extract
sat in the build context places it inside the image, so
a `.dockerignore` that excludes the data directory and an
inspection of the built image's file system are part of
the deposit. And the other artifacts must not carry
individual-level rows by another route: rendered reports,
cached chunk output, saved workspaces, logs, and test
fixtures are all places where records leak, and tables
with very small cell counts can disclose as surely as a
row does.

**De-identified data, where permitted.** Under the HIPAA
Privacy Rule, health information ceases to be
individually identifiable by one of two routes: a
qualified expert applies statistical methods and
documents that the risk of identification is very small,
or the eighteen listed identifiers are removed and the
covered entity has no actual knowledge that the remainder
could identify anyone [@cfr164514]. A limited data set,
which keeps dates and some geography, is not
de-identified and may be shared only under a data-use
agreement [@cfr164514]. NIH guidance adds that data
de-identified in the legal sense may still warrant
controlled access [@nihprivacy2026]. De-identification is
a determination made by the data's steward, not something
an analyst achieves by deleting the name column.

**Synthetic data, as a stand-in.** A synthetic file with
the same columns, types, and plausible ranges as the
analysis data lets a reader run the pipeline from end to
end and confirm that the code executes, though not that
the published estimates regenerate. It should be labeled
synthetic in the file and in the README, with the script
that generated it. A synthetic file produced by a model
fitted to the real records needs the same disclosure
review as the records themselves, since such a model can
reproduce rare individuals; one simulated from stated
parameters, as this book's running cohort is, does not.

**Controlled-access repositories.** When data may be
shared but not publicly, a controlled-access repository
holds them and releases them only to approved users under
an agreement. NIH's dbGaP, for genotype and phenotype
data, is an example: public study descriptions sit beside
an authorized-access route with its own security
procedures and code of conduct [@dbgap]. The open deposit
of code then cites the controlled-access accession, so
that the two halves are linked by identifier. The NIH Data
Management and Sharing Policy, in force since 25 January
2023, expects controlled access for data with explicit
limits on later use and asks that those limits be passed
to the repository that holds the data [@nihdms2020].

**Consent and agreement terms, read before the analysis
begins.** What may be deposited is settled by documents
signed long before the deposit: the consent form, the IRB
protocol, and the data-use agreement. The analyst reads
them for redistribution, derived data, public posting,
and retention. An agreement that requires the extract to
be destroyed at the end of the project governs every copy
of it, including those in backups, caches, and container
images. NIH guidance asks that consent explain how data
will be shared and that use agreements carry their
restrictions with the data [@nihdms2020; @nihprivacy2026].

**The data-availability statement.** The article and the
README state what was deposited, where, and how the rest
may be obtained, with the same exactness the honest-level
claim demands. A statement of the following form is
typical:

> The analysis code, package lockfile, container recipe,
> and archived container image are openly available at
> [DOI], with a synthetic dataset of the same structure
> on which the pipeline runs from end to end. The
> patient-level data were obtained from [registry] under
> a data-use agreement that does not permit
> redistribution; qualified researchers may apply to
> [data steward] for access. The synthetic data do not
> reproduce the reported estimates.

The last sentence matters for the level. A reader without
access to the data can confirm that the pipeline executes;
only someone with access can confirm that it regenerates
the published numbers, so an L3 claim must say who
performed the comparison and on what data.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: which route, and why not the obvious one

A colleague proposes removing the name and medical record
number columns from a patient-level extract and depositing
the rest openly, calling the result 'de-identified.' What
is wrong with this plan, and which of the five routes
above should be used instead?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Deleting two columns is not de-identification in the
regulatory sense: dates, small geography, and rare
combinations of remaining variables can still re-identify
a person, and a determination that the risk is very small
must be made by a qualified expert or by removing all
eighteen HIPAA identifiers, not by the analyst's own
judgment. Absent that determination in writing from the
data steward or IRB, the extract stays out of an open
deposit. The appropriate route is a synthetic stand-in with
the same structure, deposited openly and labeled as
synthetic, with the real extract made available, if the
agreement allows it at all, only through a controlled-access
repository or a direct request to the data steward.
:::
:::

### Funder and journal obligations

Everything the five routes above implement is a response
to an obligation that exists before the analysis begins: a
funder's data-sharing policy, and later, a journal's
reporting requirement. Both predate the deposit and shape
what the deposit must contain.

**The funder side.** The NIH Data Management and Sharing
Policy requires that, for proposals due on or after 25
January 2023, an applicant submit a Data Management and
Sharing Plan as part of the budget justification at the
time of application, not drafted after data collection is
underway [@nihdms2020]. NIH program staff review the Plan
for completeness rather than scoring it, but once an award
is made, the approved Plan becomes a term and condition of
that award: noncompliance can bring added special terms,
withheld funds, or termination, and can affect future
funding decisions [@nihdms2020]. The practical consequence
for the analyst is that the choice among the five routes
above is not a free one, made at deposit time. It was made,
in outline, when the grant was written, and the deposit is
the Plan's execution rather than a fresh decision.

**The journal side.** A code-availability statement is a
narrower instrument than the data-availability statement
of this section, above: it says where the *analysis code*
lives, under what license, at what version, and what it
does not include, independent of whatever the
data-availability statement says about the data. The two
statements answer different questions, and a manuscript
needs both; a reader who wants to re-run the pipeline reads
the code statement, and a reader who wants to obtain the
inputs reads the data statement.

Some reporting guidelines now name code availability as a
checklist item rather than leaving it to a journal's
general policy. TRIPOD+AI, the 2024 extension of the TRIPOD
reporting guideline to prediction models built with
regression or machine learning, lists item 18f under its
'Open science' section: 'Provide details of the
availability of the analytical code,' with a footnote
specifying that this covers the analysis code, including
any data cleaning, feature engineering, model building, and
evaluation [@collinstripodai2024]. A separate item, 18e,
asks the same question of the data. Naming code
availability as its own item, distinct from data
availability, is what makes TRIPOD+AI concrete where a
general journal policy is often vague: an author completing
the checklist cannot satisfy 18f by describing only the
data.

A code-availability statement that meets this bar states
four things: where the code is deposited, with a persistent
identifier if one was minted; under what license it is
released; which version, commit, or tagged release
corresponds to the reported results, since a repository's
default branch moves on after publication; and what, if
anything, the deposit withholds, and why (a proprietary
dependency, institution-licensed software, or data
referenced only by an accession number). 'Available on
GitHub,' without a version and a license, answers none of
the four.

## Stewardship over time

Archiving preserves the artifacts; stewardship is the
longer discipline of keeping them runnable as the world
underneath them changes. Even a carefully pinned
compendium decays. A base image tag may be re-pushed; a
package version pinned in a lockfile may age out of the
repository that once served it; a system library may be
dropped from a new operating-system release. The
question stewardship answers is: when the pins have
decayed and the archived image was lost or never built,
can the environment still be recovered?

For the R ecosystem a useful recovery tool is `rang`,
described by Chan and colleagues [@chan2023]. (`rang`
was archived on CRAN on 2026-08-22; the historical
versions remain installable from the CRAN archive or
from its GitHub repository, and the technique it
illustrates is worth knowing even if the package itself
needs an alternative source or a successor tool by the
time a reader needs it.) Where the ordinary workflow
pins prospectively, by recording a lockfile at
development time and restoring from it, `rang`
reconstructs an environment retrospectively, from a
*date*. Given the date an analysis was run, it resolves
the package versions current on the archives at that
date and generates a Dockerfile that can often
reconstruct a period-correct environment even when no
original lockfile survives. The two approaches are
complementary on a time axis: the framework of this book
enforces consistency prospectively over a project's
active life, and `rang` provides a recovery path
retrospectively when that consistency has lapsed. A
prudent steward records the
run date in the compendium precisely so that this
recovery path stays open.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

Sharing and archiving themselves reach no rung, since
preserving a level is not capturing or verifying one; the
single failure this chapter exists to prevent is depositing
a compendium no better than locatable, with a DOI and a
tidy README, and calling it 'fully reproducible' in the
article the deposit outlives.
:::

We must extend the same honesty to the tools this book
has taught, and to the framework it uses as its running
example. Frameworks that compose the whole determinant
stack are young. By its own accounting, the framework
firmly pins roughly four of the ten determinants of
computational reproducibility, the environment, the
packages, the source, and much of the session
configuration, and leaves others, the numerical
libraries, the fonts and graphics device, and intrinsic
non-determinism, to the base image or to convention. Its
own system review describes it candidly as a strong
scaffolding tool rather than a finished guarantor of
reproducibility, and notes the sustainability risk that
attends a small maintainer base: a single principal
author is a bus factor of one, and a tool maintained by
one person is a tool whose future is contingent. These
are not reasons to withhold the tool; they are reasons
to disclose its reach accurately, which is the same
discipline the honest-level callout demands of any
analysis. The evidence that disclosure cannot be taken
for granted is empirical. Stodden and colleagues,
examining the effectiveness of journal reproducibility
policies, found that the mere existence of a policy is a
weak predictor of an actually reproducible artifact
[@stodden2018]: the gap between the reproducibility a
project claims and the reproducibility it delivers is
real, common, and worth the analyst's vigilance.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: recovering a decayed environment

An analysis was run in 2024 and deposited as a source
tree and an `renv.lock`, but no Docker image was ever
built, and by 2029 several of the pinned package
versions are no longer installable from CRAN. A reviewer
asks you to reproduce it. Which tool addresses this
situation, what single piece of recorded information
does it most need, and why is this a stewardship failure
rather than a capture failure?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The `rang` package [@chan2023] addresses it by
reconstructing a period-correct environment from a date,
resolving the package versions current at that date and
generating a Dockerfile, even when the pinned versions
are no longer installable directly. The single most
useful recorded fact is the *date the analysis was run*,
from which `rang` resolves the historical package set.
It is a stewardship failure rather than a capture
failure because the pins were captured correctly at the
time (the compendium was genuinely L1). What lapsed was
the preservation of a runnable environment over time,
which an archived image or a recorded run date would have
protected. Capturing the level and stewarding it are
distinct obligations.
:::
:::

## Across the archetypes

The team and archiving machinery, the two-layer model, the
union lockfile, the registry and forge choices, the DOI
deposit, and the `rang` recovery path, is
archetype-agnostic; @tbl-archetype-weight in
@sec-compendium is the reference. What varies is the final
act of publication. A **data-analysis** or **simulation**
compendium is deposited as itself, the compendium with its
DOI *is* the published object; a **manuscript** compendium
is deposited *beside* the article it supports, cited by DOI
from its data-availability statement; a **package**
compendium has a further, ecosystem-native channel, release
to CRAN or an R-universe, whose incoming checks are
themselves a validation gate; and a **blog** compendium is
deployed as a website, with tools such as `workflowr`
[@blischak2019] binding each rendered page to the commit
that produced it, though the archival obligation still
applies to the compendium behind the posts. In every case
the underlying discipline, fix the environment, govern it
as a team, deposit with a persistent identifier, and state
the level honestly, is identical; only the last mile
differs.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the archetype that changes nothing

A simulation study, built entirely from its own generated
data, is being prepared for deposit. Which part of this
chapter's archiving machinery does it need, and which
part, unlike the manuscript and package archetypes, does
it not need to worry about?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It needs everything archetype-agnostic: the two-layer
model while the study was developed by a team, the
committed Dockerfile as the guarantee, a DOI-minting
deposit carrying the code and the archived environment,
and an honest statement of the level reached. It does not
need @sec-restricted-deposit's machinery at all, because
data generated by the study's own code from stated
parameters carries no participant, no consent, and no
data-use agreement to honor. The restricted-data callout
exists for exactly the case a simulation study is exempt
from.
:::
:::

## Worked example

We follow the multi-site cohort laboratory of the
Orientation through one quarter of collaboration and one
archival deposit, to make the abstractions concrete.

At the project's start the lead selected a base image,
resolved it to a digest, and built the team environment
once. Over the quarter, three contributors extended the
package layer independently. The union model records the
result: the project lockfile always holds the union of
every contributor's additions. The following chunk
reconstructs the running union over the quarter and
tabulates it. It uses only base R together with `tibble`
and `knitr`, and computes the cumulative union
deterministically, so it regenerates identically on
every render.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-union
#| tbl-cap: 'The renv union model over one quarter of team collaboration. Each contributor installs packages independently; the project lockfile records the cumulative union, which the shared image is periodically rebuilt from. Because it is a union rather than a running total, a package a contributor installs that another already has does not enlarge it, so the union can grow by fewer than the number of packages added. The union size never shrinks, so every contributor who rebuilds inherits the full set.'

library(tibble)
library(knitr)

contributions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~contributor,          ~added,
  'Lead (initial base)', 'here, renv, rmarkdown',
  'Ana (survival)',      'survival, survminer, here',
  'Ben (tables)',        'gtsummary, gt',
  'Cai (spatial)',       'sf, tmap'
)

added_sets <- strsplit(contributions$added, ', ')
running_union <- Reduce(union, added_sets,
                        accumulate = TRUE)

contributions$union_n <- vapply(
  running_union, length, integer(1)
)

knitr::kable(
  contributions[, c('contributor', 'added', 'union_n')],
  col.names = c('Contributor', 'Packages added',
                'Lockfile union (n)')
)
```

The table shows the invariant that makes the model work:
the union size is monotone, never shrinking as
contributors are added, so a member who rebuilds the
image at any point inherits everything the team needs up
to that point. Because it is a union and not a running
total, a package a contributor installs that the team
already has does not enlarge it: Ana adds three packages,
but one of them, `here`, was already in the lockfile from
the initial base, so the union grows by only two, from
three to five. Ana never installs `sf`, yet after the
quarterly rebuild her environment carries it, because Cai
did, and the lockfile records the union.

When the manuscript was accepted, the laboratory
deposited the compendium. The cohort's patient-level
extract came from the participating sites under a
data-use agreement that forbids redistribution, so the
deposit follows @sec-restricted-deposit: it carries the
code, the tests, the lockfile, the Dockerfile, the
archived environment, a synthetic extract with the
structure of the real one, and a README whose
data-availability statement names the sites' data
steward as the route to the real data. The extract itself
is in none of these files. The session below, shown as a
static illustration rather than executed, checks that the
image holds no study data, publishes it to a registry,
records its immutable digest, exports the environment as
a single archival file, and mints a DOI for the
compendium. The `$` prompt is not part of the commands,
and lines beginning `#>` are output.

```bash
# Rebuild the team image once, from the pinned
# Dockerfile and the union lockfile, then publish it.
$ make docker-build

# Before the image leaves the laboratory, confirm that
# no study data were copied into it; the expected
# result is an empty listing.
$ docker run --rm cohort-env:latest \
    find / -xdev -path '*raw_data*' -type f

$ docker tag cohort-env:latest \
    ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env:2026-q3
$ docker push ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env:2026-q3

# Record the immutable digest the team builds against.
# This, not the mutable tag, is the reproducible name.
$ docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' \
    ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env:2026-q3
#> ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env@sha256:4813816ad695...

# Export the environment as a single archival file for
# deposit, built from the digest-pinned image.
$ apptainer build cohort-env.sif \
    docker://ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env@sha256:4813816ad695...

# Deposit the compendium (code, tests, lockfile,
# Dockerfile, synthetic extract, README; no patient
# data) plus the archived environment in Zenodo, which
# mints the persistent identifier the article's
# data-availability statement will cite. The command is
# schematic; real deposition uses the Zenodo REST API or
# the web upload interface, and the DOI is a placeholder.
$ zenodo-upload cohort-compendium-v1.0.zip cohort-env.sif  # schematic
#> Deposited. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX
```

Three features of the session deserve note. First, the
image is pushed by a dated tag but *recorded* by digest;
the tag is convenient for humans, the digest is the
immutable name a collaborator or a reviewer builds
against. Second, the deposit carries both the compendium
and the archived environment, so that reproduction has
two independent routes, rebuild-from-recipe and
run-the-archived-image, and does not depend on the
registry surviving. Third, neither route includes the
patient data. A reader of the deposit can run the
pipeline on the synthetic extract and see that it
executes; regenerating the published estimates requires
the real extract, obtained under the sites' agreement,
and the article's level claim says so.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two routes, one reason

The deposit above includes both a rebuildable Dockerfile
and an archived SIF file of the same environment. Why
both, rather than whichever is more convenient?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because each route can fail independently, and the
deposit is meant to outlive both failures. The Dockerfile
route fails if the base image's registry disappears or a
pinned package is pulled from CRAN before `rang` or a
successor tool can recover it. The archived-image route
fails if the SIF or OCI file itself is lost or becomes
unreadable by a future runtime. Depositing both means a
reader needs only one of the two to still work, which is
cheaper insurance than it looks given how little either
artifact costs to include.
:::
:::

## The cohort, continued

The worked example above is a composite laboratory. Here
is a smaller, real question applied to this book's own
running cohort compendium: if it had to be deposited
today, what would already be true, and what would still
need doing?

```{r}
license_present <- file.exists('../../LICENSE')
description_present <- file.exists('../../DESCRIPTION')
gitignore_lines <- readLines('../../.gitignore')
raw_data_ignored <- any(grepl('raw_data', gitignore_lines))

license_present
description_present
raw_data_ignored
```

Two of the three are already in place. A `LICENSE` file is
present and dual: the prose is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and the code,
including every script that builds the cohort, is CC0,
which is the explicit license FAIR's reusability principle
asks for and which @sec-restricted-deposit's deposit example
above was silent about. A `DESCRIPTION` file is present and
records `License: CC0`, matching the code half of the
`LICENSE` file, so a package repository or an automated
check reading `DESCRIPTION` would see the same answer a
human reading `LICENSE` would. The third check returns
`FALSE`: `analysis/data/raw_data/` is not listed in
`.gitignore`, and `cohort_raw.csv` is tracked in version
control. For patient-level data that would be the single
most urgent finding in this chapter, the exact failure
@sec-restricted-deposit exists to prevent. Here it is the
correct state of affairs, precisely because the cohort is
synthetic, generated from stated parameters by a committed
script, and carries no participant to protect; the chunk
cannot tell the difference between 'correctly untracked'
and 'incorrectly tracked' on its own, which is itself worth
noting; that judgment is the analyst's, informed by what
the data actually are, not something a `.gitignore` audit
can certify by itself. What the compendium still lacks for
an archival deposit proper is the part no file-system check
can see: a minted DOI, an archived container image, and a
written statement of the level this compendium has reached
at the time of deposit.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the checks did not check

The three checks above all return favorably (or correctly
`FALSE`) for this compendium. Does that mean the compendium
is ready to deposit as L3? Why or why not?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The three checks are structural: a license file exists,
a `DESCRIPTION` agrees with it, and the data are tracked
appropriately for their (synthetic) sensitivity. None of
them is evidence that the analysis has been rebuilt from a
clean environment and its outputs compared against recorded
values, which is what an L3 claim requires. A compendium can
pass every structural check above and still be no higher
than L1 or L2, depending on whether its packages and
environment are pinned. Structural readiness for deposit and
the level honestly claimed in the deposit are two different
questions, and this section answers only the first.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for the
mechanical parts of sharing and archiving, and an
unreliable one for the parts that require judgment about
this specific project. One rule precedes the exchanges.
Patient-level, identifiable, or agreement-restricted
data, and outputs derived from them such as row-level
logs or small-count tables, are never pasted or uploaded
into a model unless the endpoint is approved by the
institution for that data; NIH, for one, forbids sharing
controlled-access genomic data with public generative AI
tools through prompts [@nihgenai2025]. A prompt about a
deposit describes the structure instead: the file names,
the column names and types, a synthetic example. A coding
agent that reads the repository reads its data too, so it
is run only in projects whose data it is allowed to see.
We give three exchanges, each with what to watch for and
what the analyst must verify.

**Prompt.** 'Write the shell commands to tag our image,
push it to GHCR, record its digest, and export it as a
SIF for archival deposit.'

*Watch for.* A model will readily produce plausible
commands, but may push and record the *mutable tag*
rather than resolving and recording the *digest*, which
silently discards the reproducibility the exercise exists
to secure. It may also invent registry paths or flags
that do not exist for your setup.

*Verification.* Run each command and confirm the recorded
reference is a `@sha256:...` digest, not a `:tag`. Pull
the image fresh on a second machine using the recorded
digest and confirm it resolves. Do not deposit until the
digest round-trips.

**Prompt.** 'Draft the data-availability and
reproducibility statement for our manuscript, citing the
deposited compendium.'

*Watch for.* The model does not know what level your
compendium actually reached, and will tend to reach for
confident language ('fully reproducible', 'all results
can be regenerated') regardless. It cannot know whether
you verified the outputs or merely pinned them. Nor does
it know the terms of your data-use agreement, and it will
often write 'all data are available in the deposited
compendium' for a deposit that holds none.

*Verification.* Rewrite the level claim yourself against
the honest-level standard: say verified only if you ran
`zzc verify` or its equivalent and the outputs matched;
say pinned if you pinned but did not re-run; name the DOI
you actually minted, not a placeholder. Check every
sentence about the data against what the deposit holds
and against the agreement, and name the access route for
anything withheld. The claim is the analyst's
responsibility, not the model's.

**Prompt.** 'Our 2024 analysis has an renv.lock but
several pinned versions no longer install. How do we
reproduce it?'

*Watch for.* The model may confidently propose editing
the lockfile to newer versions, which changes the
analysis rather than reproducing it, or may recommend
`rang` but misstate what input it needs.

*Verification.* Confirm that the proposed route
reconstructs the *original* versions rather than
substituting current ones, and that it uses the recorded
run date. Test the reconstructed environment against a
known output from the original analysis before trusting
it. A reproduction that quietly upgrades the packages is
not a reproduction.

## Exercises

1. Take an existing single-analyst compendium of your
   own and identify, for each package it uses, whether
   the decision to include it belongs to the environment
   layer or the package layer of a hypothetical team
   version. Justify the two or three borderline cases.

2. Explain, in a paragraph a collaborator could act on,
   why the committed Dockerfile rather than the pushed
   image is the reproducibility guarantee. Then describe
   one concrete situation in which relying on the pushed
   image would cause a reproduction to fail.

3. Your institution runs a self-hosted GitLab and
   forbids pushing to public forges. List the components
   of a compendium's reproducibility workflow that must
   change when moving from GitHub to GitLab, and the
   components that do not, and identify which single
   place the CI logic should live so that the change is
   minimal.

4. Deposit a small practice compendium in a research
   repository that mints a DOI (Zenodo offers a sandbox
   for exactly this). The compendium must hold no
   restricted data: use public or synthetic data only,
   such as this book's simulated cohort. Record the DOI,
   then write a data-availability statement that says
   what the deposit contains and names the level the
   compendium actually reached, defending your level
   claim against the honest-level standard. Then rewrite
   the statement for the case in which the analysis data
   were a registry extract held under a data-use
   agreement, saying what would have been deposited
   instead and how a reader could obtain the real data.

5. Take a compendium with an `renv.lock` and, using
   `rang`, generate a Dockerfile that reconstructs its
   environment from the date it was created. Compare the
   reconstructed package set against the lockfile and
   report any differences, explaining why a
   date-based reconstruction may not match a lockfile
   exactly.

6. For one archetype other than the manuscript (a
   package, a blog, or a simulation), write the specific
   'sharing with the world' step it requires beyond the
   archival deposit, and explain what validation gate, if
   any, that step adds.

7. Run the three checks from 'The cohort, continued'
   yourself: `file.exists('LICENSE')`,
   `file.exists('DESCRIPTION')`, and whether
   `analysis/data/raw_data` appears in `.gitignore` (run
   from the repository root rather than from
   `analysis/report/`, so adjust the paths). Report the
   three booleans you get, and state, in one sentence,
   which of the three findings would need to change before
   this compendium could hold real patient-level data
   instead of the synthetic cohort, and why.

8. This exercise returns to the commit rule of Chapter 4
   (@sec-version-control): never commit restricted data,
   because `git` keeps every version forever even after a
   file is deleted. The same rule turns out to apply one
   layer up. Suppose a `.dockerignore` lists `*.csv` but a
   teammate's branch adds `analysis/data/raw_data/extra.tsv`
   the week before a deposit, and nobody updates the
   ignore patterns. Walk through what happens to that file
   at each of three points, the `docker build`, the
   `docker push`, and the Zenodo deposit of the exported
   SIF, and say which single artifact, if inspected before
   the deposit, would have caught the leak.

9. Write a code-availability statement, meeting TRIPOD+AI
   item 18f's standard, for this book's running cohort
   compendium as it stands today: name the repository, the
   license (recall 'The cohort, continued' above), the
   commit or tagged release the statement should point to,
   and anything withheld. Then write the parallel
   data-availability statement for a hypothetical version
   of the same analysis built on a registry extract held
   under a data-use agreement, and say in one sentence how
   the code statement would differ from the data statement
   in that case.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. Most of
these are performed on a compendium of the reader's own, so
their outputs vary; the boxes record the criterion to apply
and the reasoning behind it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

No single correct answer. The criterion to apply is
**how often the package changes and how many contributors
need it**.

The **environment layer** holds what everyone needs and
nobody changes: the tidyverse, `knitr` and `rmarkdown`, the
plotting stack, anything requiring system libraries that
are expensive to install. Baking these into the image means
each contributor pays the install cost zero times rather
than once each, and the layer moves only when the team lead
rebuilds.

The **package layer** holds what one contributor needs for
one piece of work: a specialized survival package, a
mapping library used in a single figure, anything adopted
mid-project. These arrive through the lockfile, which every
contributor extends.

**The borderline cases** are the substance of the exercise,
and three kinds recur.

A package that *started* in the package layer and is now
used by everyone belongs in the environment layer at the
next rebuild. The signal is the union model: when a package
appears in the lockfile because several contributors
installed it independently, it has outgrown the fast layer.

A package with heavy system dependencies used by only one
contributor is genuinely ambiguous. Installing it from the
lockfile is slow and may fail without the system libraries;
baking it in imposes the size on everyone. The usual
resolution is to put the *system libraries* in the image
and leave the R package in the lockfile.

A package pinned to an unusual version for one analysis
belongs in the package layer regardless of how widely it
is used, because the image cannot carry two versions.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

A paragraph a collaborator could act on:

> The Dockerfile is a recipe and the image is a
> cake. The recipe says how the environment was made,
> in text, in version control, reviewable line by line,
> and it will still say so in ten years. The image is an
> opaque binary that someone must keep hosting. It can be
> deleted, pruned, rate-limited, or rebuilt under the same
> tag, and nothing in it explains how it was produced. So
> commit the Dockerfile and treat the pushed image as a
> cache: convenient, worth having, and not the record.

**A concrete failure from relying on the pushed image.**
Docker Hub applies a retention policy to inactive
repositories and the image is removed, or the organization
account lapses, or the tag is overwritten by a later push.
An analysis whose only environment record was that image
is now unreconstructable, and the failure appears at
exactly the moment someone tries to reproduce the work,
which is usually years after anyone was watching.

A second and more insidious failure, worth mentioning
because it produces no error: the image is rebuilt and
pushed under the same tag with a newer base. A reader pulls
the tag, gets a different environment from the one the
analysis ran in, and obtains slightly different numbers
with nothing to indicate anything moved. This is the
argument for pinning by digest as well as committing the
recipe.

A third, if the collaborator works on Apple Silicon: the
pushed image may have been built for one architecture only,
so the pull succeeds on the author's machine and fails, or
runs under emulation with different numerical behavior, on
someone else's.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

**What must change.** The CI configuration file, from
`.github/workflows/*.yml` to a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` at
the root, in the dialect of stages and scripts rather than
jobs and reusable actions. The remote URL and the
authentication method. The registry, from GHCR to the
GitLab container registry, and therefore the image
reference in any pull. The secrets, which must be
re-created as GitLab CI variables. Anything relying on a
GitHub-specific feature: pull-request comment bots,
`GITHUB_TOKEN`, Actions from the marketplace.

**What does not change.** Everything that constitutes the
reproducibility of the compendium. The Dockerfile, the
`renv.lock`, the directory structure, the `DESCRIPTION`,
the tests, the analysis code, the data dictionary, and the
checks themselves are all forge-agnostic. (Restricted
data stay off both forges; moving forges does not change
where they live.) This is the point worth
drawing out: the reproducibility machinery is not a
property of the hosting platform, and a compendium that
must be substantially rewritten to move forges was coupled
to its forge in ways it should not have been.

**Where the CI logic should live.** In a `Makefile`, or an
equivalent single entry point, so that both forges' CI
files reduce to a shim naming an image and calling
`make check`, `make render`, `make check-renv`. The
migration then touches one thin file rather than the
check logic, and the same commands run locally, which is
the incidental benefit that makes the arrangement worth
adopting even for a project that will never move.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

The deposit and DOI will differ for each reader. The
substance is the statement and its defense.

For a compendium built on simulated data, with a lockfile
and a Dockerfile but no verification record:

> The complete research compendium, comprising the
> analysis code, the simulated data and the script that
> generates them, the package lockfile, and the container
> recipe, is archived at
> https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX. The data are
> synthetic and describe no real person. The
> computational environment is pinned by a
> digest-referenced container image and an `renv.lock`
> lockfile, so the analysis can be re-executed in the
> environment in which it was developed (L2 on the
> capture ladder used in the accompanying methods). We
> have not independently verified that re-execution
> regenerates the reported outputs, so no L3 claim is
> made.

For the registry case, the deposit loses the data and the
statement gains an access route:

> The analysis code, package lockfile, container recipe,
> and archived container image are archived at
> https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX, with a synthetic
> dataset of the same structure on which the pipeline
> runs from end to end. The patient-level data were
> obtained from [registry] under a data-use agreement
> that does not permit redistribution; qualified
> researchers may apply to [data steward] for access. The
> synthetic data do not reproduce the reported estimates.
> The environment is pinned (L2); re-execution on the
> registry data has not been independently verified.

A common wrong answer keeps 'the complete research
compendium' in the second statement. It is not complete,
and saying so is part of the statement's honesty.

**Defending the claim against the honest-level standard**
means checking three things and being willing to have the
answer come out lower than one would like. Is there a
lockfile? Then L1. Is there an artifact pinning the runtime
and system libraries? Then L2. Is there *evidence* that a
rebuild regenerated the recorded outputs, a CI log, a
verification report, recorded output hashes? Only then L3.

The last clause of the statement above is the one that
makes it honest, and it is the clause most authors omit.
Omitting it does not merely leave the claim vague; it
invites the reader to assume verification that nobody
performed.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

```r
lockfile <- renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')
pkg_names <- names(lockfile$Packages)

graph <- rang::resolve(pkg_names, snapshot_date = '2026-06-29')
rang::dockerize(graph, output_dir = 'rang_build')
```

The comparison typically shows most packages matching and
a minority differing, with the differing set growing as
the gap widens between the snapshot date and the dates on
which packages were actually installed.

**Why a date-based reconstruction may not match a
lockfile exactly.** Four reasons, and it is worth
separating them.

First and most important, a lockfile records what was
*installed*, and a date reconstruction records what was
*current on a date*. These differ whenever a package was
installed on one date and the lockfile written on another,
which is the normal case for a project of any duration.

Second, packages installed from sources other than CRAN,
from GitHub at a particular commit, or from Bioconductor,
have no CRAN-dated equivalent, so the reconstruction
either misses them or substitutes something.

Third, archived packages present a gap: a package removed
from CRAN is recoverable from the archive by version but
its dependency resolution at a past date may not be.

Fourth, the reconstruction resolves the transitive closure
afresh, so a dependency that has since changed its own
requirements can pull a different set than the lockfile
recorded.

The conclusion the chapter draws: reconstruction by date
is what one falls back on when no lockfile exists, and it
is an approximation rather than a substitute. A project
with a lockfile should restore it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

Taking each in turn; the reader needs only one.

**R package.** The sharing step beyond the deposit is
publication to a package repository, CRAN or
Bioconductor, or at minimum a tagged release installable
with `remotes::install_github()`. The validation gate this
adds is substantial and externally imposed: CRAN runs
`R CMD check` across multiple platforms and R versions,
including development R, and rejects the package on
failure. This is a stronger gate than any the author
configured, precisely because the author did not configure
it, and it is the closest thing in the R ecosystem to the
independent verification of @sec-verification.

**Blog.** The step is deployment to a public URL with a
feed, and registration where readers will find it. The
gate added is thin: a deploy check confirming the site
builds and links resolve. Notably, no gate checks that the
code in the posts still runs, which is why an old post is
the most reliably broken artifact in this book's
taxonomy.

**Simulation study.** The step is depositing the full
results alongside the reduced pipeline, since the full run
is too expensive to reproduce on demand, together with the
seed and the replicate count. The gate added is the
correspondence check: the reduced pipeline under the
recorded seed must regenerate the leading replicates of
the deposited full results. That is what lets a reader
verify the machinery without paying for the study.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 7

Run from the repository root:

```r
file.exists('LICENSE')
#> [1] TRUE
file.exists('DESCRIPTION')
#> [1] TRUE
any(grepl('raw_data', readLines('.gitignore')))
#> [1] FALSE
```

The three booleans are `TRUE`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, matching
'The cohort, continued' above (there, run from
`analysis/report/`, with paths adjusted accordingly).

**What would need to change for real patient-level data.**
The third finding. `FALSE` means
`analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv` is tracked in
version control, which is correct only because the file is
synthetic. Were it a real extract, this is precisely the
commit-rule violation @sec-restricted-deposit and the
version-control chapter (@sec-version-control) both warn
against: once committed, the file is in the repository's
history forever, recoverable from any clone even after
later deletion. The license and `DESCRIPTION` findings
would not need to change; a license and a package
description are needed whether the data are real or
synthetic.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 8

**At `docker build`.** The build context includes every
file under the Dockerfile's directory not excluded by
`.dockerignore`. Because `*.csv` does not match
`extra.tsv`, the file is copied into the image by any
`COPY . .` or equivalent instruction, becoming part of
the image's file system layers.

**At `docker push`.** The image, `.tsv` included, is
uploaded to the registry as-is. The registry has no
knowledge of which files are data and which are code; it
stores the layers it is given. The leak has now left the
laboratory's own machines.

**At the Zenodo deposit.** `apptainer build` exports the
pushed image, `.tsv` and all, into the SIF file, which is
then deposited and assigned a DOI. The leak is now public
and, per this chapter's own account of archival deposits,
unrecallable.

**What would have caught it.** An inspection of the built
image's file system before the push, exactly the check
this chapter's worked example performs with `docker run
--rm ... find / -xdev -path '*raw_data*' -type f`, run
against the actual data directory rather than assumed from
the `.dockerignore` pattern. A pattern-matching ignore file
is a plan; a listing of what the built image actually
contains is a verification, and only the second one catches
a file the plan did not anticipate. This is the Verification
callout's own rule, 'how to see a claim actually holds,'
applied to the narrower claim that no data entered the
image.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 9

**Code-availability statement.** A statement meeting
18f's standard, as this book's repository stands:

> The analysis code for this compendium is available at
> [repository URL], at the commit tagged for this
> submission (not the default branch, which continues to
> change). The code is a `CITATION.cff`-bearing R research
> compendium; the code itself is released under CC0 1.0,
> and the accompanying prose and figures under CC BY-NC-SA
> 4.0. The deposit withholds nothing: the cohort analyzed
> is synthetic, generated by a committed, version-controlled
> script, and no restricted data were used.

**Data-availability statement, registry-extract version.**

> The patient-level data analyzed were obtained from
> [registry] under a data-use agreement that does not
> permit redistribution. Qualified researchers may apply to
> [data steward] for access under the same agreement terms.
> A synthetic dataset of the same structure, on which the
> pipeline runs end to end, is deposited alongside the code
> and does not reproduce the reported estimates.

**How the two differ.** The code statement answers 'can a
reader obtain and run what produced these results,' and its
answer here is simply yes, with a version and a license.
The data statement answers a harder question, 'can a reader
obtain what the code was run *on*,' and in the restricted
case the honest answer is a controlled route rather than a
download: the two statements can diverge sharply even for
the same manuscript, which is exactly why a reporting
guideline that names them as separate checklist items,
rather than one general sentence about 'availability,' is
doing real work.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-archiving}

| Command or rule | What it does or checks |
|---|---|
| `docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' <img>` | Reports the immutable digest to record, not the mutable tag |
| `docker run --rm <img> find / -xdev -path '*raw_data*'` | Confirms no restricted data were copied into the built image |
| `apptainer build out.sif docker://<img>@sha256:...` | Exports a digest-pinned image as a single archival file |
| `renv.lock` + `Dockerfile`, committed | The reproducibility guarantee; the pushed image is a cache, not the record |
| Two-layer model | Environment is lead-governed and slow; packages are contributor-governed and fast, under the union model |
| Union lockfile | Records every contributor's packages cumulatively; never shrinks; rebuild periodically, not on every install |
| `rang::resolve(pkgs, snapshot_date = ...)` | Reconstructs a period-correct environment from a date when no lockfile survives |
| Recorded run date | The single fact a retrospective recovery (`rang`) needs most |
| Restricted data (@sec-restricted-deposit) | Code and environment, always; data only de-identified, synthetic, or controlled-access, per the agreement (habit 3) |
| DOI deposit | Lifts a compendium from fragile-locatable (a forge URL) to durably findable; changes no rung on the ladder |
| Honest claim at deposit | State the rung actually reached; the deposit outlives the memory of what was done (habit 7) |

## Further reading

- Wilkinson and colleagues [@wilkinson2016] formulate
  the FAIR principles for research data; Barker and
  colleagues [@barker2022] adapt them for research
  software, whose reuse involves execution. Read both to
  understand what an archival deposit is trying to
